note: The ii–V–I built from the major scale, then heard: tap every other note of the staff from the three ringed starting notes, then name each chord on a backing track. The chords are chord tokens counted the long way once, the staff rings only the notes the text names, a listening drill for any instrument hears its chords from a backing-track, and the key is moves with a {{?key}} line on what stays the same.

exercise.title: The ii–V–I, built from the scale
exercise.why: Stacking every other note of the major scale on its 2nd, 5th and 1st notes builds the three chords of a ii–V–I, so you can find them in any key from the scale alone.

cells.text:
The staff below shows the {{=key}} major scale: tap a note to hear it. Start on the ringed {{2}} and tap every other note going up until you have four: that is {{chord:ii7}}, the 2nd chord of the key, built on {{2}}.
Do the same from the ringed {{5}} for {{chord:V7}}, the 5th chord, built on {{5}}, and from the ringed {{1}} for {{chord:Imaj7}}, the 1st chord, built on {{1}}.
Practice until you can find the four notes of each chord without counting them out.

Press Play below to start the backing track: {{chord:ii7}}, {{chord:V7}}, then two bars of {{chord:Imaj7}}. Say the number of each chord as it arrives: 2, 5 or 1.
Listen for the bar of {{chord:V7}}: it pulls toward {{chord:Imaj7}}, and the 1st chord sounds like home when it comes.
{{?key}}In another key the three chords have other names, and they still come from the 2nd, 5th and 1st notes of the scale.
